notes.meaning: Exactly one month after leaving Egypt, the Israelites move from the oasis of Elim into the dry Desert of Sin on their way to Mount Sinai. By this time, the food supplies they carried out of Egypt have run out. God brings them into this barren land so they can learn to depend directly on Him.

With their supplies gone, the entire community turns against Moses and Aaron and begins to complain bitterly. Instead of praying to the God who parted the Red Sea, fear spreads quickly through the camp. When hard times come, complaining against leaders is often a sign of a heart that has stopped trusting God.

The people cry out that they would rather have died in Egypt by the pots of meat and full loaves of bread than starve in the desert. They accuse Moses and Aaron of dragging them into the wilderness to kill them. In their panic, they romanticize the cruel days of slavery and imagine the past was much better than it really was.

God tells Moses that He will rain bread down from heaven to feed the people every single day. The people must go out and gather only enough for that day so God can test whether they will trust and obey His directions. God answers their bitter complaining with kindness, showing His mercy to an unworthy people.

On the sixth day of the week, the people will prepare what they bring home and find it is twice as much as on the other days. This extra supply prepares them for the weekly day of rest. God takes care of their needs in advance so they will not need to work on His holy day.

Moses and Aaron tell all the Israelites that food will arrive that very evening. When they eat, they will know beyond doubt that the Lord delivered them from Egypt, not their human leaders. God gives them this proof to quiet their doubts and confirm His saving power.

In the morning, the people will see the shining glory of the Lord in the miraculous gift of bread. Moses reminds them that God has heard every word of their grumbling. Because Moses and Aaron are only servants doing God's will, complaining against them is really complaining against God.

Moses explains that the Lord will give them meat at twilight and plenty of bread at dawn because He has heard their complaints. God hears every discontented word, even when spoken quietly inside a tent. Moses repeats that their anger is aimed directly at the Lord, who controls all things.

Moses tells Aaron to call the entire congregation to come near before the Lord. God summons them like a judge calling people into a courtroom because He has heard their rebellious words. Standing before God helps people realize how serious their complaints truly are.

While Aaron speaks to the assembly, the people turn and look out toward the empty desert. Suddenly, the bright and awesome glory of the Lord flashes out from within the guiding cloud. This powerful sight reminds the grumbling people that God is present, holy, and fully in control.

The Lord speaks to Moses and confirms that He has heard the cries of the Israelites. He tells Moses to promise them meat at twilight and plenty of bread in the morning. Through this faithful supply, the people will know that the Lord is their personal God who cares for them.

That evening, a large flock of quails flies into the camp, landing so thick and exhausted that the people catch them easily. The next morning, a heavy layer of dew surrounds the entire camp. God fulfills His promise immediately by providing fresh meat for dinner and preparing the ground for breakfast.

When the morning dew evaporates, tiny thin flakes remain on the desert ground like white frost. This substance was completely new to the people and lay spread out across the dry sand. God used the moisture of the dew to deposit clean, fresh food directly from above.

The Israelites see the flakes and ask one another, 'What is it?' because they have never seen anything like it before. Moses tells them that this is the heavenly bread the Lord has given them to eat. God often provides for His people in surprising ways that they do not recognize at first.

Moses gives the people God's rules for collecting the manna. Each person is to gather one omer, which is about two quarts, for every member of their tent. This instruction made sure that every person received a fair and healthy portion of food.

The people go out to gather, with fast workers collecting more and weaker people collecting less. Yet when they measure the food back in camp, those who gathered much have nothing left over, and those who gathered little have no shortage. God supernaturally blesses their gathering so that every family has exactly what they need.

Moses commands the people not to save any of the manna overnight for the next morning. God wants them to rely on His care fresh each day rather than hoarding food. Leaving leftovers would show that they doubted whether God would feed them tomorrow.

Some of the people ignore Moses and hoard manna overnight, but by morning it fills with worms and stinks. Moses becomes very angry at their lack of faith and open disobedience. Trying to keep God's blessings against His commands only turns good gifts into rottenness.

The Israelites quickly learn to rise early each morning to collect what they need. As the desert sun grows hot, whatever manna is left lying on the ground melts away. This daily schedule taught them to be diligent and not delay in taking what God provided.

On the sixth day, the people gather food and discover they have twice as much as usual, two omers for each person. The community leaders are surprised by this and come to tell Moses what happened. God faithfully fulfills His promise to give them a double harvest ahead of time.

Moses explains that the next day is a holy Sabbath, which means a sacred day of complete rest dedicated to the Lord. He tells them to bake or boil whatever they need for two days and set aside the rest for tomorrow. Preparing their food ahead of time allows them to focus entirely on resting with God.

The people save their extra food until morning just as Moses told them to do. Unlike the spoiled manna from earlier in the week, this portion stays completely fresh and has no worms or bad smell. God protects and preserves whatever is kept in simple obedience to His word.

Moses tells the people to eat the stored manna because the seventh day is the Lord's Sabbath. He warns them that no food will fall in the fields that day. Six days are given for gathering and labor, but the seventh day belongs to God as a time of rest.

In spite of Moses's clear warning, some of the people still go out into the desert on the seventh day looking for manna. They search the ground, but find nothing at all. Their actions show how difficult it is for anxious hearts to stop working and trust God's promises.

The Lord asks Moses how long the people will refuse to obey His commandments and laws. Even though Moses was faithful, God addresses him as their leader so he can firmly correct the disobedient crowd. God cares deeply about obedience, even in small, practical instructions.

Moses reminds the people that the Sabbath is a gift from the Lord, which is why He gives them two days of bread on the sixth day. Because God has provided for them, each person must stay in camp and not go out looking for work. The Sabbath was given to bring peace and relief, not stress.

The people finally listen to God's instruction and rest on the seventh day. Seeing that no food appeared, they stop searching and accept the day of quiet. True rest comes when people cease their own striving and depend on what God has provided.

The Israelites call this heavenly food manna, which remembers their question, 'What is it?' It looks like small white coriander seeds and tastes sweet like wafers made with honey. God did not feed them tasteless survival rations, but pleasant and nourishing bread.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern writers have suggested manna was the sweet gum that drops from tamarisk shrubs in the Sinai peninsula, but commentators point out that natural gum cannot be baked or ground into flour and never appears in amounts large enough to feed a nation.

notes.meaning: Moses announces that God wants one omer of manna saved in a jar for all future generations. This kept sample would allow their children and grandchildren to see the actual bread God used to feed their ancestors in the wilderness. Remembering past miracles helps future generations trust God with their own lives.

Moses commands Aaron to take a jar, fill it with an omer of manna, and place it before the Lord to be preserved. Unlike the manna that rotted overnight, this special jar would stay fresh through the centuries. God turned this simple food into a lasting witness of His goodness.

Aaron obeys the Lord's command and places the jar before the Testimony, which refers to the sacred chest of the covenant built later. The jar of manna sat alongside God's written law as a constant reminder of His loving care. God wants His people to remember both His holy commands and His gracious provisions.

The Israelites eat manna every day for forty full years as they journey through the wilderness. The heavenly supply continues without failing until they reach the borders of the settled land of Canaan. God faithfully provides for His people during long seasons of waiting until their journey is complete.

The account closes with a brief note explaining that an omer is one-tenth of an ephah, equal to about two to three quarts. This helpful note allowed later readers who used different measurements to understand the exact size of each person's daily share. It shows that God was generous and gave everyone plenty of food each day.
